questions.q: Define "wardrobe planning" and list the five sequential steps in the process as per CBSE Class 12 Home Science curriculum.
questions.a: Correct answer: Wardrobe planning is the systematic process of evaluating clothing needs and managing apparel resources. The five steps are: 1) Wardrobe audit (inventory and condition check), 2) Needs analysis (lifestyle, climate, occasion mapping), 3) Gap identification (comparing inventory vs. needs), 4) Acquisition strategy (budgeted purchasing plan), 5) Maintenance and review (care, repair, periodic reassessment). A wrong answer that lists "shopping" as step 1 reveals the misconception that planning starts with buying rather than assessing what already exists — this leads to duplication and budget waste.

questions.q: A student says: "Capsule wardrobe just means owning fewer clothes — like minimalism." Explain why this statement is incomplete and identify the TWO defining operational criteria that distinguish a capsule wardrobe from merely a small wardrobe.
questions.a: Correct answer: A capsule wardrobe is defined by (1) Interchangeability: every top must coordinate with every bottom and layering piece, creating multiple outfits from few items, and (2) Seasonal rotation: it is rebuilt each season (typically 3 months) with a fixed item count (e.g., 33 items), not just permanently small. A wrong answer focusing only on "fewer clothes" misses the mathematical combinatorics — a 10-item random wardrobe yields fewer outfits than a 10-item capsule where each piece matches 3 others. This misconception leads students to simply discard clothes without building a functional system.

questions.q: Priya (22, college student, Mumbai) has ₹8,000 budget for summer wardrobe update. Her audit shows: 3 cotton kurtas (good), 2 jeans (1 tight, 1 good), 1 formal shirt (worn), 0 trousers, 0 dupattas, 2 sandals (1 broken). She needs: daily college wear (4 days/week), weekly presentation (1 day), weekend casual. Apply the 5-step process to create her acquisition priority list with estimated costs.
questions.a:
Step 1 Audit: Keep 3 kurtas, 1 good jeans. Discard tight jeans, worn shirt, broken sandal.
Step 2 Needs: College (4 days) = 4 casual tops + 2 bottoms; Presentation (1 day) = 1 formal shirt + 1 trouser; Weekend = 1 casual dress/kurta + 1 bottom.
Step 3 Gaps: 0 trousers (need 2: 1 formal, 1 casual), 0 dupattas (need 2 for kurtas), 1 formal shirt, 1 sandal.
Step 4 Acquisition priority (budget ₹8,000): 1 formal trousers ₹1,200, 1 cotton trousers ₹800, 2 dupattas ₹600, 1 formal shirt ₹1,000, 1 sandal ₹1,500 = ₹5,100. Remaining ₹2,900 for contingency/accessories.
Step 5 Review: Monthly check fit/wear. Wrong answer buying 3 trendy tops first reveals failure to prioritize foundational gaps (trousers, formal shirt) over variety — violates needs analysis.

questions.q: Compare the wardrobe planning factors for: (A) A 16-year-old school student in Delhi vs (B) A 35-year-old software engineer in Bengaluru. Analyze how climate, dress code, budget autonomy, and body changes differentially weight the factor "versatility" in their capsule wardrobes.
questions.a: Correct analysis: (A) Delhi student: Extreme seasons (summer 45°C, winter 5°C) require two distinct capsules; school uniform reduces daily versatility need but increases need for versatile non-uniform items (coaching, weekends); low budget autonomy (parent-funded) favors durability over trend; rapid body changes (puberty) demand adjustable fits (elastic, oversized). Versatility weight: MODERATE — uniform handles weekdays. (B) Bengaluru engineer: Mild climate (15-28°C) allows single year-round capsule; no uniform means daily professional versatility critical (meetings, video calls, commute); high budget autonomy enables quality investment; stable body allows tailored fits. Versatility weight: VERY HIGH — each piece must work for 5+ contexts. Wrong answer treating both identically ignores how dress code and climate fundamentally alter the "cost per wear" calculation that drives capsule logic.

questions.q: Evaluate this capsule wardrobe proposal for a working woman in Chennai: 5 neutral tops (white, beige, navy, black, grey), 3 bottoms (black trouser, navy pencil skirt, beige chinos), 1 blazer, 1 cardigan, 1 trench coat, 2 dresses (black, printed), 2 shoes (black loafers, nude heels), 1 tote. Critique using the criteria: colour harmony, occasion coverage, climate suitability, and combinatorial math (minimum outfits).
questions.a: Critique: Colour harmony: Good — neutrals + 1 print, but missing accent colour for visual interest (add 1 coloured top). Occasion coverage: Gap — no ethnic wear for Indian festivals/formal events (add 1 kurta set). Climate suitability: FAIL — trench coat useless in Chennai humidity; cardigan too heavy; replace with 1 linen shirt-jacket and 1 cotton shrug. Combinatorial math: Tops (5) × Bottoms (3) = 15 base combos; +2 dresses = 17; ×2 shoes = 34 outfits before layers. With blazer/cardigan: 34×2 = 68 theoretical. But climate mismatch reduces actual wearable outfits by ~40%. Wrong evaluation calling it "perfect" ignores that a capsule must be wearable in the user's actual climate — theoretical combinatorics ≠ functional utility.

questions.q: Design a 10-piece monsoon capsule wardrobe for a male college student in Kolkata (budget ₹6,000) using ONLY quick-dry fabrics. Specify each item with fabric, colour, approximate cost, and justify how it creates ≥25 distinct outfits. Include a "stress test" scenario (sudden formal event) and show how the capsule adapts.
questions.a: Good answer example: 1) Navy quick-dry polo ₹600, 2) Grey quick-dry polo ₹600, 3) Olive quick-dry tee ₹500, 4) Black quick-dry tee ₹500, 5) Khaki quick-dry chinos ₹900, 6) Navy quick-dry shorts ₹700, 7) Grey quick-dry joggers ₹800, 8) Packable rain jacket ₹1,200, 9) Quick-dry towel-shirt (dual use) ₹600, 10) Waterproof sneakers ₹1,600 = ₹8,000 (over budget — must adjust: remove joggers, use shorts+chinos only = ₹7,200 still over; final: drop rain jacket, use poncho ₹200 = ₹6,200). Combinatorics: 4 tops × 2 bottoms = 8 base; + towel-shirt as layer = 8×2 = 16; + rain jacket/poncho as outer = 16×2 = 32 outfits. Stress test: Formal event — wear navy polo + khaki chinos + rain jacket (structured) = business casual. Poor answer lists cotton items (slow dry) or ignores budget — shows failure to integrate material science with planning constraints.
